position: Legislative and cross-agency priorities for other departments
proposal: Among its cross-agency requests, the Mandate asks the State Department to quickly impose stiff sanctions on recalcitrant countries until they actually accept deportees, not merely promise to. It asks DOJ either to move the immigration courts to DHS or to treat immigration judges and Board of Immigration Appeals members as national security personnel, decertify their union, and hire significantly more. The same list also covers housing, education, labor, Treasury and intelligence items that this record does not track.

status_summary: Executive Order 14159, section 13 (signed 2025-01-20), directs State and DHS to apply INA section 243(d) visa sanctions to countries that refuse removable nationals, the Laken Riley Act (approved 2025-01-29) lets states sue the Secretary of State over a failure to apply them, and on 2025-04-05 the Secretary of State announced revocation of all visas held by South Sudanese passport holders and a halt to new issuance over South Sudan's failure to accept timely returns (the statement cites no statute, so its link to section 243(d) is an inference). For the immigration judges' union, the Federal Labor Relations Authority had already excluded immigration judges from their bargaining unit as management officials in 2020 and 2022, before this period; the only later step found is EO 14251 of 2025-03-27, which excludes the Department of Justice as a whole from the federal labor-management relations program without naming EOIR, and no outcome of the judges' renewed bid to restore the union (reported in December 2024) and no step moving EOIR to DHS were found. On 2025-08-28 EOIR published a final rule letting the Director designate any attorney as a temporary immigration judge for renewable terms of up to six months. A CRS Insight of 2026-03-02 reports that permanent immigration judge numbers fell from 735 at the end of FY2024 to 557 at the end of the first quarter of FY2026 and notes that Public Law 119-21 funds immigration judge hiring with a ceiling of not more than 800 judges from 2028-11-01, while EOIR announcements of 2025-10-24 and 2026-02-05 named 11 permanent and 25 temporary immigration judges (courts in 16 states) and then 6 permanent and 27 temporary immigration judges (courts in 15 states); a significant increase in permanent hiring was not found.

timeline.event: Executive Order 14159 was signed; section 13 directs the Secretaries of State and Homeland Security to apply INA section 243(d) sanctions where appropriate and to remove barriers to prompt returns, weighing delayed identity confirmation.

The Laken Riley Act (Public Law 119-1) was approved; section 3(c) adds a subsection to INA section 243 letting a state attorney general sue the Secretary of State for injunctive relief over a failure to discontinue visas as required by section 243(d).

Executive Order 14251 was signed, listing the Department of Justice as a whole among agencies excluded from the federal labor-management relations program; it does not name EOIR or immigration judges.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced revocation of all visas held by South Sudanese passport holders and a halt to further issuance, saying South Sudan's government had not fully accepted timely return of citizens the United States seeks to remove.

title: Sanction countries that refuse deportees; decertify the immigration judges' union
uncertainties: The page 167 list is heterogeneous, so this record covers the sanctions item and the immigration judges' union item; the EOIR transfer is tracked in c05-01, the Labor wage-level item in c05-07 and the Intelligence Community item in c05-14, and the HUD, Education and Treasury items are not tracked and need their own research. The South Sudan statement was read through a hosted copy because state.gov did not load. A Cuban delegation visa denial reported in February 2026 under section 243(d) comes from a tracking site summary of a newspaper report and is not used. For the union element, the decertification events (FLRA 2020 and 2022) predate this period; the only event since 2025-01-20 is EO 14251's DOJ-wide exclusion, which does not name EOIR or immigration judges, and a search found no FLRA ruling on the restoration petition. Whether any 2025 DOJ action treats judges as national security personnel was not found. A 2026-10-19 check found no FLRA or court action on the immigration judges' union or on EO 14251 as it touches EOIR in the sources reachable (results were from 2020 to 2022 or 2024), and no further 243(d) sanction announcement beyond South Sudan from a primary source; one low-quality aggregator article on 2026 country lists was not used. The CRS Insight was read through the everycrsreport.com mirror and its headcount stops at the end of the first quarter of FY2026 (2025-12-31); the EOIR announcements of 2025-10-24 and 2026-02-05 were opened on justice.gov on 2026-10-22 (by the researcher and re-opened in review) and are now dated events; both notices were read only for their headlines, dates, counts, states and appointing authority. Whether designating temporary judges counts toward the hiring item is a judgment call; it adds adjudicators without raising the permanent corps. A 2026-10-19 re-check opened a printout of the South Sudan statement on assets.aila.org (state.gov did not load): it cites failure to cooperate on returns but no statute, so tying it to section 243(d) is an inference. It also opened two Authority orders on flra.gov in the immigration judges' case (72 FLRA No. 121 of 2022-01-21 and No. 146 of 2022-04-12), which concern the management-official exclusion and not a restoration petition. An external retrieval reported that a restoration petition was filed on 2022-07-21, that a hearing was held in December 2024 and that no Regional Director decision is public; this was not verified against an opened document and differs from the record's reference to a December 2024 petition, and the news article the record cites on that point could not be opened in this check. The retrieval's further claims (no other section 243(d) action since 2025-01-20, and a March 2025 FLRA rule on representation authority) are likewise unverified. An external retrieval reports an EOIR Adjudication Statistics table (generated July 2026) showing 662 immigration judges on board in the third quarter of FY2026, 192 hired in FY2026 to that point, 53 temporary judges on board at 2026-06-30 and 634 on board for FY2025; these figures were not opened and are not used. If confirmed they would bear on the remaining item on permanent hiring and on the statement that no significant increase in permanent hiring was found, since they could indicate a rise from the 557 permanent judges reported by CRS for the first quarter of FY2026, depending on whether the 662 includes temporary judges. The announced permanent investitures (11 and 6) are small beside the CRS decline from 735 to 557.
